ASTM · a VSA cognitive map for Spot
Replay English Time Merge How it works Limits

The whole room, remembered in four vectors

A Boston Dynamics Spot walked one lap of a classroom. All 4,498 object detections along the way — what each one was, where the robot was, when it happened — were multiplied into four fixed-size 8192-dimensional complex vectors. There is no landmark list, no pose graph and no database of detections: recall is arithmetic. You divide out the parts of the question you know, and correlate what is left against a grid to read off the part you do not. Every panel below is a real query, run offline on a laptop CPU in single-digit milliseconds and exported here as static results.

Start anywhere. Three things worth trying: press play on the replay below; click “cold storage for food” in the English panel; drag the time slider and watch the memory abstain. The mechanism is explained after the demos, not before them.

How to read this page

  • The bright blobs are memories, not pictures. Each heat map is a similarity field: how strongly the memory believes the answer is at each point on the floor. Dark purple = no, bright yellow = yes.
  • Ring = ground truth, cross = what the memory said. The gap between them, in metres, is printed next to every panel.
  • Similarity numbers are small on purpose. They are normalised by the 8192 dimensions, so compare them to each other (and to the z score against the noise floor), never to 1.0. z < 3 means the memory is abstaining — saying “nothing here” rather than guessing.
  • There are two memories on this page, not one. The replay and time panels query four traces built from the robot's own pose stream. The English panel queries a second memory of identical construction, built over object positions with text-derived class atoms. Same algebra, different traces — so “where” means the robot's vantage in one and the object's location in the other.
  • Nothing loads from the network. The images, fields and numbers are baked into this one file, so it works offline or over a shared link. It is a static export: the queries were run ahead of time, and nothing is computed as you scrub.
8192-dcomplex FHRR vectors; 4 traces hold the whole walk
512 KBof traces — flat in the number of detections (but not the whole footprint: see limits)
3–10 msmeasured per time-query on a laptop CPU; no learned decoder
0.15 mmedian position recall over the replayed walk

2 · Ask it in English

A sentence you never taught it, used directly as the key

The map stores object classes from a detector — chair, tv, suitcase. It has never seen the phrase “cold storage for food”. Here we take the raw sentence-embedding of the phrase, whiten it, and hand it to the memory as the unbinding key, with no lookup table and no retraining. Click a phrase.

This panel queries a second memory, not the four traces from the replay above: same algebra and same dimension, but built over object positions (from depth) with class atoms derived from the class names rather than from random seeds. So “where” here means where the object is, not where the robot stood. The five-step pipeline is diagrammed below ↓

true object location decoded peak other objects in the room

 

Closest stored class labels (text similarity)

How the sentence actually gets in (and what that does not mean)

Five fixed steps, no lookup and no retraining. (1) all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeds the phrase into 384 real dimensions. (2) That embedding is whitened by a PCA fitted over the vocabulary — the 38 detected class names plus 203 further common object nouns, 241 rows in all — keeping up to 128 unit-variance components. (3) A single fixed Gaussian matrix W ~ N(0, 1/din) of shape (din, 2D) turns it into (I, Q) pairs. (4) Each pair is normalised onto the unit circle and its magnitude discarded, leaving an ordinary unit-modulus phasor of dimension 8192. (5) The memory is unbound by that phasor and the residual correlated against the position grid.

The step that makes it work: the memory's class atoms were built with the same encoder, the same whitening and the same W, from the class names. So a novel phrase lands near the atoms of semantically similar class names, in the same phasor space the map is written in.

What this is not: the language model never reads the map, and nothing is decoded back into text. The sentence is projected into the map's own space and then it is just algebra. Note that this cuts both ways — the projection has no notion of which chair you meant, so on a class with many instances the answer is whichever mode of the similarity field happens to be highest. See the annotated pipeline ↓

What you are looking at. The heat map is the memory's answer to a question posed in free-text English, with the sentence vector itself acting as the algebraic key — the phrases were never stored, never enumerated, never trained on. Why it is interesting. 9 of the 11 phrases land within 0.25 m of the object we scored against (median error 0.19 m). The two that miss, miss differently, and the difference matters. “A computer display” is 5.93 m from the tv we scored against but lands 0.10 m from a laptop — a genuinely semantic miss, and arguably the better answer. “Something to sit on” is 6.93 m from the chair we scored against but lands 0.14 m from a different chair: the right class, the wrong instance. That is not a language failure at all. chair has 23 instances scattered round the room, the similarity field is multi-modal, and a single argmax has to pick one peak. It is the failure mode any argmax over a multi-instance class will always have, and fixing it needs instance identity in the memory — which is not built. The five-step projection, diagrammed ↓

3 · Ask it about time

Where was it then, and when was it there

Time is bound in as a third factor, so the same four vectors answer questions in both directions. Divide out the class and the timestamp to get a map of where; divide out the class and a place to get a curve over when. The time key is a complex exponential whose similarity kernel is a smooth sinc-like bump, and an entire window of time integrates in closed form into a single key — so asking about a 28-second window (a third of this 83-second walk) costs about what asking about a single instant costs: 9.8–10.2 ms against 9.0–10.2 ms.

robot pose at t nearest sighting of this class decoded peak

A time range, for the same price: “where was the chair during…”

“What moved between the first third of the walk and the last?”

The answer: classes the memory is actually confident about

The foil: top-5 by raw displacement, confidence ignored

Every one of these is at the noise floor — z < 3 in both windows, the highest reaching only 2.70. Rank a 38-class vocabulary by displacement without checking confidence and you are ranking crosstalk. This is why the abstention flag exists.

What you are looking at. One fixed-size memory answering where-given-when (top) and when-given-where (middle) and what-changed-between-two-windows (bottom) — all by division and correlation, never by scanning a log. Why it is interesting. A time range costs about what a time point costs, because the window integrates in closed form into a single unbinding key. And the abstentions are visible rather than hidden: person clears the confidence threshold at only 1 of 10 time points. Seven of those nine abstentions are honest — no person was detected anywhere near those instants. Two are misses. At t=275 and t=963 there were 35 and 16 person detections within one time length-scale and the memory still said nothing. person contributes 383 events against chair's 2,369, and rare classes lose to crosstalk. The abstention flag is well calibrated, not infallible. Why crowding a memory blunts every answer ↓

4 · Two memories, one sum

Merging two maps is addition

This walk's 4,498 detections are split alternately into two halves, and each half is built into its own memory. Add the two together and you get, exactly, the memory you would have built from the union — agreement to 3.9×10−15, i.e. floating-point noise. The merged memory is the same size as either input: k sessions still occupy 512 KB, tested to k=16. Be clear about what this is: a clean test of the algebra's additivity, not two robots covering different ground. Interleaving means both halves see the whole room.

If B's coordinate frame is offset by an unknown amount, one correlation sweep over candidate offsets recovers it, and the offset is then divided out of B's memory before adding. That is the whole procedure. The sweep here returns the true (+1.40, −0.90) m offset exactly — but that is partly the luck of the grid, which steps in 0.1 m and happens to contain the answer. Read it as accurate to the sweep resolution, not as accurate to zero.

No ICP, no landmark matching, no data association — correspondence is implicit in the algebra, because identical content lands on identical vectors and simply sums. Two preconditions make that work, and both are real constraints. The two memories must share the same random bases and the same class codebook; and both must weight by confidence alone, because class-frequency weightings depend on global counts and are not additive. The English-query memory on this page uses one of those weightings, and so is not mergeable as built. We have also not benchmarked scene-graph or kNN fusion, so read this as an architectural contrast rather than a measured win.

What you are looking at. Two independently built memories and their sum, compared against the ground-truth joint memory. Why it is interesting. Map fusion is one vector addition plus one correlation sweep, at constant memory cost, with no correspondence problem to solve first — subject to the two preconditions above. Why a coordinate offset divides out cleanly ↓

5 · Under the hood

How it actually works

You have just watched it work. Here is the whole mechanism, with no metaphors: a place, a heading and a moment are each turned into a list of angles, one angle per dimension, and the only things ever done to them are add the angles, average the vectors and subtract the angles. The four widgets below are not illustrations — they run the real construction, live, as you move the controls.

Read this first. The widgets in this section build their vectors at D = 1024 dimensions with their own random draw, so that the kernel shape and the interference between stored items are big enough to see on a screen. The exported memory everywhere else on this page is D = 8192 with a different draw. The formulas are the same, but these widgets are an independent JavaScript re-implementation checked against the Python — not the production code path itself. Every number printed below is computed in your browser as you read it, rather than baked in.

1 · Position: every dimension is a clock

Position uses fractional power encoding. Two base vectors Bx and By are drawn once: each of their dimensions gets a random phase from Uniform(0, 2π), and the stored value is exp(i·phase) — a point on the unit circle. Raising such a vector to a fractional power just multiplies its phase, so encoding a place is one line:

ctx_pos(x, y) = (Bx ** (x / l)) * (By ** (y / l)) l = pos_length_scale = 0.75 m S(x, y)[m] = exp( i * ( phi_x[m] * x/l + phi_y[m] * y/l ) )

Every one of the 8192 dimensions is a little clock, and each clock's hand turns at its own fixed rate as you move in x and in y. No single number holds the position: it is held in the pattern of phases across dimensions. Drag the sliders and watch the pattern change smoothly.

64 of the 1024 clocks

Hand = that dimension's phase. Shade = cos(phase), which is exactly that dimension's contribution to the similarity with the room origin S(0, 0). Average that over all 1024 dimensions (only 64 are drawn) and you have the number printed below.

Similarity to “here”, across the room

the point you chose room origin (0, 0)
   

A straight-line slice through that blob

slice along x slice along y dashed: your point’s similarity to the origin
 

What to notice. The blob follows you, but its shape never changes — the similarity between two places depends only on the displacement between them, never on where in the room they are. That translation-invariance is the homomorphism, drawn. The bump's width is set by the length scale l = 0.75 m — precisely, it falls to half height at 0.30 l ≈ 0.23 m and first crosses zero at l/2 = 0.375 m, so the marker drawn at l itself sits on the second null, not on the edge of the bump. l is the resolution dial for the whole map.

The two consequences, written out

(a) It is a homomorphism, so displacement is native. Phases add under binding, and binding is an elementwise complex multiply, so S(a) ⊗ S(b) = S(a+b) exactly — the readout above measures the largest per-dimension disagreement and finds only floating-point rounding, which shrinks to a single unit in the last place of a double once the phases involved are small. Run it backwards and you get the useful one: S(target) ⊘ S(anchor) = S(target − anchor). A relative displacement is not a special case that had to be built — it falls out of the encoding.

(b) The similarity kernel is a bump whose scale is set by l. sim(S(0), S(d)) = (1/D) ∑m cos(phim · d/l). With phases drawn uniformly this is a sinc-like bump: nearby places are similar, distant places are near-orthogonal. That kernel is the reason every heat map on this page is a blob rather than a single lit pixel, and it is why a coarse decoding grid can still be read out sensibly. Shrink l and the bump narrows: more resolution, less tolerance to error, and more stored items needed to cover the same room.

2 · Heading: a circular base, not a ring attractor

This one is worth stating plainly, because it is easy to assume otherwise: there is no ring attractor network and no continuous attractor network anywhere in this implementation. Heading uses the same fractional power encoding as position, with one change to the base vector. In circular_base, each dimension is given a random integer frequency k drawn from {−3,−2,−1,1,2,3}, and the base stores exp(i·k):

ctx_head(psi) = Bhead ** psi Bhead[m] = exp(i * k[m]), k[m] integer, 1 <= |k[m]| <= 3 (Bhead ** psi)[m] = exp( i * k[m] * psi ) => ctx_head(psi + 2*pi) == ctx_head(psi)

Because every k is a whole number, a full turn returns the vector to exactly where it started. An ordinary uniform-phase base does not do that — turn all the way round with one of those and you arrive at a stranger. Flip the toggle to see the difference.

Similarity to heading 0, one full turn

the heading you chose ordinary base (when shown)

The same curve, unrolled over two turns

circular base (what the code uses) ordinary uniform-phase base
 
 

What to notice. Two things at once. The curve has several lobes, not one clean peak — that is the whole explanation for the lumpy petal shape in the heading panel of the replay above. And the circular curve is identical to floating-point precision at −2π, 0 and +2π, while the ordinary base's is not: turn a full circle with an ordinary base and the memory thinks you are somewhere new.

Why |k| ≤ 3, and why the shape is lumpy

Why 3. Bhead ** psi is a complex power, evaluated on the principal branch: it computes exp(psi · log(Bhead)), and log returns an imaginary part in (−π, π]. The integer frequency k only survives that round trip while |k| < π. Three is the largest integer that fits, which is why max_freq is 3 and not, say, 12.

Why the lobes. The kernel is (1/D) ∑m cos(km · Δψ), and with only three magnitudes available it is a sum of harmonics 1, 2 and 3 — in expectation (cos Δψ + cos 2Δψ + cos 3Δψ) / 3. That is a truncated Dirichlet-style kernel: a main peak at zero, a trough below zero near π, and side structure in between. A position code, whose phases come from a continuum, has no such ceiling and gets a much cleaner single bump. Exact periodicity is bought with angular sharpness, and the polar panel in the replay is that trade-off on screen.

On ring attractors, said carefully. Ring and continuous attractor networks are the standard neuromorphic way to hold a heading. Closely related is the GC-VSA work of Krausse, Neftci, Sommer & Renner (NICE 2025, arXiv:2503.08608), whose algebra is inspired by continuous attractor networks and VSAs — though it models grid-cell position coding rather than heading. The representation here is from the same family; the difference is that this code computes the vector directly rather than letting a network settle into it, and a continuous attractor network is the natural hardware implementation route for exactly this algebra. But nothing on this page runs one, and no result here should be read as evidence about one.

3 · Bind, bundle, unbind — and what it costs

Three operations, and that is the entire vocabulary. Bind is an elementwise complex multiply, i.e. add the phases: it is invertible and it destroys similarity, so a bound pair looks like nothing in particular — which is what makes it usable as a key. Bundle is the elementwise mean: it superposes, keeps the result the same size no matter how many things go in, and preserves similarity to each ingredient — at the price of accumulating interference. Unbind is an elementwise divide, i.e. subtract the phases.

bind(a, b)[m] = a[m] * b[m] phases add (invertible, destroys similarity) bundle(v)[m] = mean_i v_i[m] superposition (D wide however many go in) unbind(a, b)[m] = a[m] / b[m] phases subtract (the inverse of bind)

Below, k object atoms are each bound to a place code and bundled into one trace; then the trace is unbound by one of those atoms and the residual is compared against all 40 place codes. Slide k and watch the margin close.

Similarity of the residual to each of the 40 place codes

the place we asked for the other 39 (crosstalk)

Margin (signal ÷ crosstalk) as more items are stored

measured margin dashed: √(2D / k), the prediction
 
dimensions D
 

What to notice. Both numbers shrink as k grows, because bundling is a mean — but they shrink at different rates: the signal falls like 1/k while the crosstalk falls only like 1/√(kD), so the margin between them closes like √(2D/k). Leave D at 1024 and the right answer still wins at k = 40, but only by 2.1× over the loudest competitor rather than 20×. Drop D to 64, push k to 40, and it stops being the top match at all. That one curve is the capacity of the entire scheme, and it is why this page keeps quoting z scores rather than raw similarities.

4 · How an English sentence becomes a key

The language section below is the same algebra with one extra front-end. Nothing is decoded into text and no language model reads the map; the sentence is simply projected into the very same phasor space the map was written in, and then divided out. Five steps, all fixed once the vocabulary has been embedded:

step 1
Sentence → embedding
all-MiniLM-L6-v2 maps the phrase to one dense vector.
384-d real
step 2
Whiten by PCA
PCA fitted over the vocabulary — the 38 detected class names plus about 180 common object nouns — keeping up to 128 components, each rescaled to unit variance.
≤128-d, isotropic
step 3
Fixed random projection
One Gaussian matrix W ~ N(0, 1/din), drawn once, of shape (din, 2D), giving an (I, Q) pair per dimension.
2D = 16384 reals
step 4
Throw the magnitude away
Each (I, Q) pair is normalised onto the unit circle. Only the angle survives — an ordinary phasor, indistinguishable in type from a place code.
D = 8192 phasor
step 5
Divide, then correlate
The memory is unbound by that phasor and the residual is correlated against the position grid. Pure algebra from here on.
M ⊘ φ(text)

The step that makes this work is the one easiest to skip over. The memory's class atoms were built with the same encoder, the same whitening and the same W, from the class names. A phrase the map has never seen therefore lands near the atoms of semantically similar class names, in the same space, and unbinding just works. The whitening is not cosmetic either: raw sentence embeddings are strongly anisotropic, and without isotropising them first the projected phasors are too mutually similar to unbind cleanly.

This also explains the shape of the failures. Over the 11 phrases on this page the median position error is 0.19 m, and the two that miss — “something to sit on” (6.93 m out, landing on the couch) and “a computer display” (5.93 m out, landing on the laptop) — miss semantically, not mechanically: the embedding genuinely ranked a different but plausible object first, and the memory answered the question it was actually asked. There is no live language model in this page — step 1 was run offline and its results inlined, which is why this panel is a diagram rather than a text box.

6 · Honest limits

What this page does not show

  • One room, one walk. Every number here comes from a single classroom sequence. A second environment was attempted and abandoned: on school_run1 the LIO-SAM odometry diverged (209 pose jumps over 5 m), giving a 118 m position error that measures the odometry rather than the memory. Nothing on this page demonstrates generalisation across environments.
  • Nothing is held out. Every replayed step and every time point queries frames that are in the stored set. This measures faithful recall of what was written, not prediction, not generalisation, and not robustness to anything unseen.
  • The ground truth is estimator-matched, not independent. “True” object positions come from the detector's own class map and “true” robot positions from the same pose stream that was encoded — and the kernel-density estimator that produces them uses the encoder's own length scales (0.75 m in space, 20 frames in time). A de-circularising bandwidth sweep was applied to one benchmark only, not to the numbers on this page.
  • The deployed footprint is dominated by the decoder grids, not the traces. The four traces are 512 KB at D=8192. For the exact configuration shown here the decoder grids are 414 MB and the total map state is 420 MB. A coarser D=4096 configuration totals 118 MB, with 256 KB of traces. “The map is half a megabyte” is true of the memory and false of the machinery you need to read it.
  • The speed is a property of the decoder, and the storage economics do not yet favour this. Decode is 91% of query time (0.32 ms encode, 0.05 ms unbind, 4.89 ms decode at D=8192) — the “one unbind and correlate” framing hides that the correlate is nearly all of it. On bytes, an exact event table overtakes the traces at about 3.3k events, already passed at the 4,498 demonstrated here; an indexed table answers in ~1.8 µs and is never beaten on latency. The honest case for this representation is compositional query, not storage economy — and testing that properly against a vector-database baseline is the next milestone, not a settled result.
  • Whitening is a constant factor, not a scaling law. Whitening the keys buys roughly 22× on the crosstalk-growth metric (4.6× on a recall-relative one). It does not change how crosstalk grows with load: measured slopes are +0.97 raw against +0.86 whitened. It moves the curve down; it does not bend it. Every number on this page also uses whitening statistics fitted offline over the whole walk — a causal, online version is about 10× worse (0.86 m against 0.09 m whole-walk L1).
  • A single argmax cannot separate instances of a class. chair has 23 instances in this room, tv 10, person 10. The similarity field is multi-modal and the readout takes one peak, so “where is the chair” has no well-posed answer. This is the cause of the language miss above, and no instance identity is stored anywhere in the memory.
  • Relational predicates are not implemented. “The chair next to the desk”, “the bag under the table” — none of that exists here. The algebra supports class, place and time, and that is all that has been built.
  • The core algebra is not ours. vsa.py — the phasor type, bind, bundle, unbind and the random projection — is ported essentially verbatim from neuromorphs/VSACognitiveMapping. What is added here is the multi-trace spatio-temporal layer, the calibration and abstention machinery, the language projection and the evaluation.

Running it yourself

Code: github.com/neuromorphs/VSACognitiveMapping, branch astm. The replay and time panels run vsa_cognitive_mapping/astm_traces.py (TraceSet, QueryRouter.query(decode, what=, where=, when=)) against outputs/classroom/astm_traces.pt. The English panel runs vsa_cognitive_mapping/language_query.py (LanguageMap), which builds its own memory from outputs/classroom/events_object.csv rather than loading those traces. The merge result comes from vsa_cognitive_mapping/memory_merge.py, and the crosstalk figure from vsa_cognitive_mapping/crosstalk_scaling.py.

This page is a static export: every field, peak, similarity, z-score and latency was produced by running the query code on the classroom data, then quantised to 8-bit and inlined here. Nothing is simulated, and nothing is fetched at view time — the page makes no network requests of any kind. Two caveats for anyone trying to reproduce it: the widgets in “Under the hood” are a JavaScript re-implementation that recomputes in your browser, and the export script that generated this file is not yet committed to the branch, so the page is currently reproducible only from the underlying modules and data.
